discoveries.headline: South Korea drafts its big new crypto law
discoveries.why: South Korea's financial regulator released its draft digital asset law on 24 November, and it puts banks in charge of won stablecoins. Digital Today's Sangyeop Oh explains the detail: exchanges need approval and face a 20 percent cap on any one shareholder, won stablecoins start with bank-majority consortiums only, and domestic token sales (ICOs) would return with a white paper filed with the regulator. A useful look at how one of the world's busiest crypto markets is writing its rules. Education, not advice.

discoveries.headline: Sheikh Hasina sets a date to go home
discoveries.why: Bangladesh's deposed prime minister Sheikh Hasina plans to return from exile in India on 16 December, the anniversary of the end of the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson told Reuters. She faces a death sentence passed in absentia, and a minister says she would be arrested and jailed on arrival. A short, clear read on a homecoming that could test Bangladesh's new government.

discoveries.headline: A fish with a see-through head, in 4K
discoveries.why: Scientists from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute filmed a barreleye fish 600 metres down off California, only the eleventh time they have met one in nearly 40 years of dives. Its tubular eyes sit inside a clear dome of tissue and can turn to keep prey in sight, and the team watched it for about 20 minutes. One of the ocean's strangest faces, up close.

discoveries.headline: Jon Kabat-Zinn on trusting the present moment
discoveries.why: Jon Kabat-Zinn, who created Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, reflects on trusting the present moment, and on how mindfulness lets us meet life's "full catastrophe" with openness, clarity and wisdom. Stress often comes from living ahead of ourselves, so this is a gentle way to land in the morning before the day takes off. The first of three free dialogues from Lion's Roar.
discoveries.meta_credit: Lion's Roar · Dialogue 1 of Jon Kabat-Zinn Brings Mindfulness to Life

discoveries.headline: Ishtar, goddess of love and war
discoveries.why: In Our Time explores Ishtar, known as Inanna in Sumerian, a goddess of love and of war who was worshipped across Mesopotamia for more than 3,500 years. Misha Glenny and three scholars from Pisa, Oxford and Leicester ask why her contradictory roles made her so powerful, and what she meant to kings. A rich 53 minutes for the commute.
discoveries.meta_credit: In Our Time · Misha Glenny with Martin Worthington, Christopher Metcalf and Selena Wisnom

discoveries.headline: Vivian Pham brings The Coconut Children to the stage
discoveries.why: Western Sydney writer Vivian Pham wrote her debut novel The Coconut Children in high school, and now she has adapted it into a play running at Belvoir St Theatre from 21 November to 20 December. She tells Mia Abrahams how the stage version moves faster, gives Vietnamese a bigger role, and draws on her father's experience as a refugee. A warm interview with a young writer to follow.

discoveries.headline: Ayurveda for a calmer festive season
discoveries.why: As the end-of-year rush builds, Ayurveda teacher Stacey Ramsower offers simple ways to stay steady: keep a routine ("Vata loves boundaries"), soothe each of the five senses, and make a wish list of things to give yourself. It's practical and kind, with nothing to buy. General information, not medical advice.

discoveries.headline: Seventeen minutes of gentle yoga for sleep
discoveries.why: Yoga teacher Juliana Berfield leads a gentle flow designed to settle you into calm before bed, from Dana-Farber Cancer Institute's Zakim Center sleep and relaxation toolkit. Save it for tonight: an easy evening ritual to close the day. If sleep is a real struggle, talk to your doctor.
discoveries.meta_credit: Dana-Farber Cancer Institute · Zakim Center · Juliana Berfield, PhD, E-RYT 500

discoveries.headline: The farmer's carry: pick it up and walk
discoveries.why: Dr Şule Eren explains why carrying a weight in each hand is one of the most useful strength moves there is, and how to do it safely. Beginners can start with about a quarter to a third of body weight per hand, three to five carries of 20 to 40 metres, two or three times a week, with shoulders back and short, quick steps. Keep breathing, and check with your clinician first if you have heart or blood-pressure concerns.
discoveries.meta_credit: Acibadem International · Dr. Şule Eren, MD
